en.title: Dicevaders: Your Next Roguelike Obsession Is Rolling In
en.summary: Forget endless grinding; a new roguelike deckbuilder demands precision dice rolls for alien invasion success. This compelling loop has already hooked players, promising deep strategy.
en.body:
The roguelike genre is saturated, but **Dicevaders** is proving that a simple, elegant core mechanic can still capture players' imaginations. This compelling dice-based deckbuilder, set in the **StarVaders** universe, has already sunk its claws into early adopters, with many finding themselves compelled to sneak in "just one more run" before the workday begins.

Players assume the role of an alien invasion captain, tasked with decimating planetary defenses. The battlefield is a grid, and success hinges on strategically placing units and then rolling three dice. Each die's outcome corresponds to a column on the grid, activating the units within. The core loop involves drafting units for specific columns, rolling your dice, and seeing which columns score based on their strength stats and any multipliers applied. A successful invasion requires hitting a target damage number within four turns; failure results in taking damage each subsequent turn until the run ends. The game also features artifacts that can significantly alter scoring, boost unit strength, or increase multipliers, adding layers of strategic depth and replayability.

What sets **Dicevaders** apart is its emphasis on *perfecting* the dice rolls and the synergy between units. Unlike many roguelikes where luck can feel overwhelming, here players have agency in shaping outcomes through unit placement and artifact acquisition. The **StarVaders** universe provides a familiar visual and thematic backdrop, with **Dicevaders** sharing its grid-based combat and promise of endless replayability. This familiar foundation, combined with the addictive dice-rolling mechanic, makes it easy to see why players are already comparing it favorably to other genre titans.

## A Fresh Take on Deckbuilding

While the premise might sound familiar on paper – a roguelike deckbuilder with a grid and dice mechanics – **Dicevaders** distinguishes itself through its unique scoring system and the player's ability to influence dice outcomes. The goal isn't just to have strong units, but to have them activated by fortunate rolls, or to build synergies that make *any* roll a good roll. For instance, a network of "Swarmers" might share a giant strength stat with adjacent units of the same type, effectively multiplying their score regardless of the specific number rolled on the dice. This focus on *how* you activate your units, rather than just *what* units you have, is where the true strategic depth lies. It’s a constant dance between mitigating bad luck and maximizing good fortune, a challenge that keeps players hooked.

## The Appeal for Dedicated Fans

For fans of games like **Balatro**, the "just one more run" compulsion is a familiar and welcome sensation. **Dicevaders** taps into that same addictive loop, offering a satisfying blend of risk, reward, and strategic planning. The ability to draft units, acquire powerful artifacts, and then see how your carefully laid plans interact with the randomness of the dice creates a dynamic and engaging experience. The game’s connection to the existing **StarVaders** IP also provides a built-in audience eager to explore more of that universe, especially with mechanics that promise deep replayability. It’s a game that respects players' intelligence, rewarding thoughtful play without shying away from the inherent thrill of chance.

## What's Next

The full version of **Dicevaders** is anticipated for a 2026 release on Windows PC and Mac. A demo is currently available for players eager to experience the addictive dice-rolling mechanics and strategic deckbuilding before the official launch.

content_raw: This is how I knew Dicevaders got its claws into me: the first thing I did this morning was boot up my Steam Deck (which is next to my bed, of course), just so I could get another run in before logging on for work. This kind of compulsive behaviour hasn't been part of my daily routine since Titanium Court back in May, and before that, Blue Prince in 2025—so Dicevaders is in good company. You play the captain of an alien invasion force hurtling through the stars in this roguelike deckbuilder, which is about activating units on a grid using three dice. Each column on the grid corresponds to a number on the dice. You draft your units in each column, roll the dice, then the outcome determines which columns of units will score. As you can see below: (Image credit: Playstack/Pengonauts) Your units don't actually go anywhere or fight anything. They each have a strength stat which forms the base score of each turn. Let's say you roll a pair of threes and a six, as I did in the screenshot above. Your units placed in the third column will have their strength stat multiplied by two, while the unit in the sixth column will only score its basic strength stat because one dice only equals a 1x multiplier. The goal is to hit a target damage number across four turns, which successfully triggers the invasion. If you don't hit the number, you start losing health on each further turn until it's game over. Of course, you can also buy a suite of artifacts which positively affect the score in many ways, from increasing multipliers to bolstering the permanent strength stats of your different units. Written down, all of this sounds pretty familiar. And it is! But what's key to Dicevaders' appeal is how much scope it gives you to affect both the outcome of each dice roll and your current run. Sure, chance is a factor in how you play, yet there's an intensive resource management layer here that makes it feel fair. For example, you have a currency called 'Budge', which is self-explanatory: you can spend one Budge point to move a dice roll either up or down one per turn (so, a four becomes a five or three), and you can do this for all three dice. You can also spend another currency called 'Chrono' to re-roll the dice completely. That gives you quite a bit of scope to avoid the dice roll landing on the columns with all your dud units. Both of these resources are finite. The game isn't that stingy with them, however, and you have numerous ways to get more, which is what gives Dicevaders its feeling of fairness. In between each turn, you're given cash to spend on units, artifacts and both these vital currencies. You can also freeze an item to buy it on the next turn if you're short on cash—again, all of this adds to the feeling that the developers want to give you the power to turn your luck around, rather than write off a run early.
